newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: KPMG says NAB retains top bank position.
newsitem.headline: KPMG says NAB retains top bank position.

text.p: Accountancy firm KPMG said in its 15th annual Australian financial survey that Melbourne-based National Australia Bank Ltd had again been ranked as the top bank but warned that banks would face continued competition which had reduced overall profit growth in 1996.
KPMG said NAB was the clear winner based on profit performance, return on assets, and its high quality lending portfolio.
It was followed by Commonwealth Bank of Australia, Westpac Banking Corp and the Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd.

KPMG said while the top two positions were unchanged, ANZ and Westpac had switched rankings with the latter bank improving its ratio of write-offs to loans and also achieving the highest net profit growth of the big four banks in 1996.

It ranked the top four regional banks as Bank of Melbourne Ltd, which is under a friendly bid from Westpac, Advance Bank, Trust Bank and Bank of Queensland Ltd. Advance Bank was taken over by fifth-ranked St George Bank Ltd in January this year. The top four "other banks" or investment banks were Bank of Singapore, Bankers Trust, Citibank and Macquarie Bank Ltd.
Australian banks' net profits rose by 9.8 percent or A$611 million in 1996, KPMG said.

"Whilst this is a strong performance the slowdown in the growth in profitability has been significant. In 1995, total banks' profits grew by A$1.2 billion representing a 23 percent increase over the previous year," the accountancy firm said.
A table in the KPMG survey showed that 1996 bank profit growth was the slowest since 1989's 2.5 percent increase. This period, however, included overall losses in 1990 and 1992.
KPMG said the top four banks increased 1996 net profit by 10.4 percent and the regional banks by 8.6 percent.
KPMG said banks and other financial institutions which had a heavy reliance on the residential mortgage market would struggle to maintain profitability.

"Regional banks, building societies and to a lesser extent credit unions are under the greatest threat due to their dependence on residential lending," it said. "While they must meet the market on pricing of both assets and liabilities they do not appear to have great scope to reduce costs."
KPMG said the impact of the mortgage rate war among the banks and non-bank originators would not be evident in the next round of bank profit results.

"A full financial year effect of these cuts will not be seen until 1998. The major banks' half year results which will be released over the next few days are unlikely to reveal a significant deterioration in this regard," KPMG said.
NAB, Westpac, and ANZ all work on a September 30 balance date and are due to release their 1996/97 first half profits to March 31 in the next few weeks. Commonwealth Bank works on a July-June year.
